facility_roles.note: The Tunka-133 array is one of the setups of the Tunka valley facility.
facility_roles.quote: in the Tunka valley 50 km to the west from Lake Baikal (51.49 N, 103.04 E)

intervals.label: Tunka-133 operation
intervals.note: The April 2021 arXiv text says the array "is taking data since 2009"; the TAIGA collaboration's 2022 overview says "in 2012 we finished deployment of the Tunka-133 array" (six satellite clusters were added in 2011). No later statement that the array is still running was read, so "active" with an open end is the last reported state.

quantity.quote: arranged over an area of 3 km2
The Tunka-133 array is located at an altitude of 670 m a.s.l.

name: Tunka-133
notes: No separate Tunka-133 collaboration is named: its papers are by members of the TAIGA collaboration, whose lecture describes Tunka-133 as one of the TAIGA facility's setups, so collaboration:taiga is referenced.

Tunka-Rex (digital radio array, deployed 2012), Tunka-Grande (scintillators from KASCADE-Grande, 2014-2015) and Tunka-21cm are further setups of the same facility; they are described inside experiment:taiga and not given their own records.

physics_goals.quote: permits a detailed study of energy spectrum and mass composition of cosmic rays in the energy range from 6 · 1015 to 1018 eV
physics_goals.value: Measure the energy spectrum and mass composition of primary cosmic rays from 6 × 10¹⁵ to 10¹⁸ eV.

summary.plain: Tunka-133 is a field of 175 light detectors in a Siberian valley that watch, on clear moonless nights, for the blue flash of air showers made by cosmic rays near the knee of the energy spectrum.
summary.technical: EAS Cherenkov-light array of 175 optical detectors in 25 clusters over about 3 km2 at 670 m a.s.l. in the Tunka valley; operating since 2009, measures the all-particle energy spectrum and mass composition from 6 × 10¹⁵ to 10¹⁸ eV (7 seasons published). Part of the Tunka/TAIGA facility.
